If A is traveling fast from the reference frame of B, A will age slower than B. But from the viewpoint of A, B is traveling fast and thus aging slower. The situation only stops being symmetric if one of the two accelerates. Special relativity only works when considering stuff from an inertial frame of reference.

Something can only be motionless relative to something else. There is no absolute frame of reference, and from any given point, everything is going to be in motion that isn't somehow attached to that frame of reference. You're sitting still at your computer, reading this, as I am writing this. We're at rest relative to one another. Both the interior and exterior of the set are being coloured with the same algorithm, here. The overall concept is to set the red channel equal to floor(255* (2-abs(z.real)/2))%256. Green uses z.imag, and blue uses the absolute value of z in it's entirety. Once those coordinates have been obtained, your project them into the HSV colour space. RGB colours work by describing a colour as the amoutn of red, green, and blue making that colour - eg, red is 255,0,0; green is 0,255,0; and blue is 0,0,255. By contrast, HSV encodes what the color is in a circle, how vibrant that colour is, and how bright it is. Relevant to this algorithm is the last number, the value, which determines brightness. To generate this image, one takes the value and subtracts it from it's maximum amount (eg, if valMax = 100 and val = 70, then you subtract 70 from 100). Then, you set the result of that subtraction to be the new value, and project the HSV coordinates back into RGB colour space. This image is the final result.

You basically need 2 skills - programming, and a basic understanding of complex algebra. Anyway, some articles I particularly remember are

How to Plot The Mset By Hand - insight into what the mandelbrot algorithm does
Wikipedia on Colouring Algorithms - information on how to make basic colouring algorithms so you can translate the output of running a mandelbrot set loop into an output format suitable for an image.
Netpbm Format - This wikipedia article has everything you need to know to output your program's information into an image.

Note that if you output to ppms, colours will be determined in the RGB colourspace - see my post above for a bit on that, search for more, or play around in Pain or some other image program's colour picker to get a feel for it.
